groups.heading: Applies almost everywhere
items: Privacy notice. Needed as soon as the site collects an email (mailing list, ticket alerts, downloads) or an enquiry. It names who collects, what, why, how long and how to unsubscribe or ask for deletion.

Mailing-list consent. Marketing emails generally need prior opt-in in the EU, UK and Israel; the US uses an opt-out model with conditions. An email gate for a free download is a marketing signup and must say so.

Copyright in the music. Publishing a recording of a cover song generally needs a licence from the song's publisher (often a mechanical or synchronisation licence for video). Embedding official players from streaming services is generally how artists share music without hosting files. Not verified per country.
Lyrics are protected text; reproducing them needs permission from the publisher.
Photos belong to the photographer unless assigned; publishing needs a licence and usually a credit.

Ticket resale. Many countries regulate secondary ticketing and above-face-value resale. One reference states that transfer and resale are only through the official face-value platform (observed 2026-11-22).

Merchandise sold on the site makes the act a shop: prices with tax as required, delivery, returns, a withdrawal right for distance sales in some places. One reference's footer carries terms, returns and exchanges, shipping and a "withdrawal request" link (observed 2026-11-22).
Performing for hire: a written contract with deposit, cancellation, timings, power and space needs, sound limits and what happens if the band cannot play.

groups.heading: Israel
items: Accessibility: websites of businesses serving the public must be accessible, with an accessibility statement and a contact, under the Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law and its regulations, with Israeli Standard 5568 as the technical reference. Whether a musician's site counts as a business serving the public, and small-business exemptions: not verified.
Privacy: the Protection of Privacy Law applies to a mailing list; Amendment 13 came into force in August 2025. Not verified for a musician's list.
Marketing messages: the "spam law" (section 30A of the Communications Law) requires prior consent for advertising by email or SMS. Believed to apply to a band's newsletter; not verified.
Copyright: the Copyright Act 2007; collective licensing through ACUM for authors and composers. How it applies to cover recordings on a band's site: not verified.

groups.heading: European Union and United Kingdom
items: GDPR and UK GDPR apply to mailing lists and enquiries. Cookies: consent for non-essential cookies (ePrivacy, PECR); embedded players may set cookies. Not verified in detail.
UK: the Consumer Rights Act 2015 sets information duties on secondary ticket resale. Believed true; not verified.
Distance-selling withdrawal rights apply to merchandise; tickets for a dated event are usually excluded. Not verified.
Copyright collecting societies (for example PRS for Music in the UK) license performance and recording rights. Not verified for a band's own site.
Accessibility: the European Accessibility Act from June 2025 covers some e-commerce; microenterprise exemption; scope for a band's merch store: not verified.

groups.heading: United States
items: CAN-SPAM sets rules for commercial email (identification, opt-out, physical address). Believed true; not verified in detail.
Text-message signups (one reference shows a text-message number on its home page, observed 2026-11-22) fall under the TCPA, which requires prior express consent for marketing texts. Not verified.
Mechanical licences for cover recordings are available under a statutory licence. Not verified in detail.
Several states regulate ticket resale and ticket-price disclosure (all-in pricing). Not verified per state.
State privacy laws (for example California) may apply above thresholds. Not verified.

platform_rules: The product may generate the structure of a privacy page (with a mailing-list heading), shop terms if merchandise is sold, booking terms for a band for hire, and an accessibility statement, each marked as a draft that needs review.

groups.heading: Applies almost everywhere
items: Fundraising is regulated in most countries: who may ask for money, what must be disclosed, and how donor data is used.
Donor data: names, addresses, amounts, payment history are personal data; giving to some causes can reveal beliefs or health, which are sensitive data in many places.

Website accessibility statement under the Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law regulations; exemptions by size. Not verified for small associations.
Privacy Protection Law, Amendment 13 (in force August 2025): duties for donor databases. Not verified.

groups.heading: Applies almost everywhere
items: The person's own data. Publishing one's own details is the person's choice, but the product should not encourage over-sharing (rules 1 and 2). Information about other people in posts (friends, family, colleagues) can raise privacy and defamation questions.
Privacy notice. Needed as soon as the site collects other people's data: a contact form, a newsletter, comments, analytics with cookies.
"Household" exemption. Data-protection laws often exempt purely personal or household activity. A public website that collects visitors' data is generally believed not to fall under it. Not verified.
Newsletter consent. Marketing or regular emails need prior agreement and an easy unsubscribe in most places.
Affiliate links and sponsored posts must be disclosed in many jurisdictions.
Copyright. Quoting others is allowed within limits (fair use, fair dealing, quotation exceptions) that differ by country. Images from elsewhere need permission. Not verified per jurisdiction.
Defamation. A personal site is publishing. Statements about named people can be defamatory. Not legal advice; the product does not judge content but should not generate claims about third parties.
Comments. Hosting other people's comments may bring responsibility for removing unlawful content once notified. Not verified per jurisdiction.

groups.heading: Israel
items: Privacy: the Protection of Privacy Law applies to stored data such as newsletter lists. Amendment 13 came into force in August 2025. Whether and how it applies to an individual's site: not verified.

Marketing messages: section 30A of the Communications Law (the "spam law") requires prior consent for advertising messages. Whether a personal newsletter counts as advertising depends on its content: not verified.
Accessibility: the duty to make websites accessible applies to those providing a service to the public. Whether a private person's non-commercial site is covered: not verified, believed not.
Defamation: the Prohibition of Defamation Law applies to online publication. Not verified in detail.

groups.heading: European Union and United Kingdom
items: GDPR (EU) and UK GDPR apply to newsletter lists and contact forms on a public site; the household exemption is believed not to cover them. Non-essential cookies need consent (ePrivacy rules in the EU, PECR in the UK).

Germany: a legal notice (Impressum) with the operator's name and an address is believed to be required for sites that are not purely private, which can include a personal blog with ads or affiliate links. This conflicts with keeping a home address private; a service address is sometimes used. groups.heading: Applies almost everywhere
items: Privacy notice. Needed as soon as the site collects a name and a phone number (a booking, an enquiry, a newsletter). Reference 1 states under its newsletter field that subscribing means agreeing to receive promotional content under its privacy policy (observed 2026-11-21).

Allergy notes are health data in many places, which is more strictly protected. Default: the booking form asks the guest to tell the staff; if a note field exists, it is kept only as long as the booking.
Allergens. A restaurant must be able to tell a guest which listed allergens are in each dish. The form differs by country.
Prices. Whether menu prices must include tax, and how a service charge must be disclosed, is set by law in most places.
Alcohol. Selling it needs a licence; promoting it has age rules.
Terms. Needed when the product takes deposits, card holds, vouchers or prepaid events: cancellation, no-show fee, refund, voucher expiry.
Marketing messages need prior agreement. A booking confirmation is not marketing.
Reviews and awards must be real and current.

groups.heading: Israel
items: A restaurant requires a business licence under the Business Licensing Law, with Ministry of Health conditions. Details: not verified.
Kosher: presenting a restaurant as kosher without a certificate from an authorised body is prohibited under the Kosher Fraud Prohibition Law. Which bodies are authorised today: not verified.
Prices shown to consumers must include VAT (Consumer Protection Law). Not verified for menus specifically.
Service: whether a mandatory service charge is allowed, and how tips must be handled for wages and tax: not verified.
Calorie and nutrition labelling duties for restaurant chains: not verified.
Allergen disclosure duties for restaurants: not verified.

Accessibility: the website of a business serving the public must be accessible and carry an accessibility statement, with exemptions for very small businesses by turnover. Thresholds and current standard version: not verified.
Privacy: the Protection of Privacy Law applies to booking data; Amendment 13 came into force in August 2025. What it requires of a single restaurant: not verified.
Marketing messages: prior consent under section 30A of the Communications Law. Details: not verified.
Gift vouchers: rules on minimum validity exist. Details: not verified.
Sale of alcohol to minors is prohibited and a notice is required on premises. Whether a website needs anything: not verified.

groups.heading: European Union and United Kingdom
items: EU Regulation 1169/2011 lists 14 allergens and requires that information on them be available for non-prepacked food, including restaurant dishes; member states decide the form. The UK kept the list. Believed true; not verified against the text.
UK, England: businesses with 250 or more employees must show calories on menus, since April 2022. Small restaurants are outside it. Not verified.
UK: from 2024-2025, tips and service charges must be passed to staff in full under the Employment (Allocation of Tips) Act. What must be said on a menu: not verified.
UK: a discretionary service charge must be shown clearly before ordering under consumer-protection rules. Not verified.
Displayed consumer prices must include VAT: believed true in both; not verified.
UK: the Food Hygiene Rating must be displayed in Wales and Northern Ireland, and is voluntary in England. Not verified.
GDPR and UK GDPR apply to booking data. Consent is needed for non-essential cookies. Reference 4 states on its page that it uses cookie-free analytics (observed 2026-11-21).
Distance-selling cancellation rights have an exception for catering and leisure services booked for a specific date. Whether a prepaid restaurant booking falls under it: not verified.
European Accessibility Act, from June 2025, with a microenterprise exemption. Whether a restaurant booking page is in scope: not verified.

groups.heading: United States
items: Menu prices usually exclude sales tax and tip. Some states and cities regulate added service fees and require them to be disclosed up front. Not verified per place.
Federal menu-labelling rules require calories on menus of chains with 20 or more locations. Not verified.
Nine major allergens are named in federal law for packaged food; restaurant duties come from state and local food codes. Not verified.

The Americans with Disabilities Act is applied by courts to restaurant websites in many cases. Reference 7 ends its page with a line offering help by phone to anyone having trouble using the site (observed 2026-11-21).
Liquor licensing is by state and locality. Not verified.

platform_rules: The product asks which country the restaurant is in before generating any legal page or price format.
The product may generate the structure of a privacy page, terms and an accessibility statement, each marked as a draft that needs review.
The product never writes "licensed", "kosher", "halal", "allergen-free" or "complies with" on its own.

groups.heading: Applies almost everywhere
items: Privacy notice as soon as the site collects a name and phone. Booking data for foreign visitors may cross borders.
Health data: dietary allergies and mobility needs may count as health data in many places. Collect only what the tour needs, and say why.
Terms whenever the product takes bookings or money: cancellation by visitor, cancellation by the guide, weather, minimum numbers, lateness, refunds.
Photos of visitors need consent before publication.
Reviews must be real.
Insurance: guides commonly carry public liability insurance. Whether it is required and whether it must be stated: not verified.

groups.heading: Israel
items: Guiding tourists in Israel is believed to require a licence from the Ministry of Tourism. Whether this applies to every kind of guided walk, and whether the licence must be shown on a website: not verified.

Accessibility of the website: the Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law and its service-accessibility regulations require an accessibility statement for businesses serving the public, with exemptions for very small businesses. Thresholds: not verified.
Displayed prices to consumers include VAT; whether tours sold to foreign tourists are VAT-exempt and how prices must then be shown: not verified.
Distance-selling cancellation under the Consumer Protection Law: how it applies to a dated tour: not verified.

groups.heading: European Union and United Kingdom
items: GDPR (EU) and UK GDPR apply to booking data; non-essential cookies need consent.

The Consumer Rights Directive is believed to exclude leisure services booked for a specific date from the 14-day withdrawal right, so the operator's own cancellation terms govern. Believed; not verified against the text for this file.

The Package Travel Directive (EU) 2015/2302 and the UK Package Travel Regulations may apply when a tour is sold together with accommodation or transport. A single-day guided tour is believed not to be a package. Not verified.
Guide licensing differs by country and sometimes by site. Italy, Greece and others are believed to require a licensed guide inside certain monuments and museums. Not verified per country.
European Accessibility Act: whether a small tour operator's booking page is in scope: not verified.

groups.heading: United States
items: Some cities have required tour-guide licences in the past and some of these rules were challenged in court. Current rules per city: not verified.
ADA applied to websites by courts in many cases; no single federal technical standard for private businesses. Not verified.
Sales tax on tours varies by state. Not verified.

groups.heading: Applies almost everywhere
items: Privacy notice. Needed as soon as the site collects a name and contact.

Children's data. Data about minors is more protected in many places, and online services aimed at children may need a parent's consent below a set age. Default: the product collects a minor's details only through the parent.
Learning needs and diagnoses may be health data. Default: not collected unless the customer decides to, and then private.

Safeguarding. Working one-to-one with children brings duties and expectations (background checks, lesson in a visible place, no private messaging with a child). Which are legal duties and which are good practice differs by country.
Terms. Lesson cancellation, missed lessons, course refunds and transfers, minimum numbers, shown before the parent or student pays.
Distance purchases. Online enrolment may carry a cooling-off right; recorded online courses may have a different rule once access starts.
Copyright. Exam papers, textbooks and worksheets belong to their owners. Recording lessons needs the participants' agreement.
Advertising claims. Results and qualifications must be true and evidenced.
Marketing messages generally need prior agreement.

groups.heading: Israel
items: Accessibility: websites of businesses serving the public must be accessible with an accessibility statement and a contact, under the Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law and its regulations, with Israeli Standard 5568 as the technical reference. Small-business exemptions exist. Not verified in detail.
Privacy: the Protection of Privacy Law applies; Amendment 13 came into force in August 2025. Not verified for a one-person tutor.

Work with minors: a law on preventing the employment of sex offenders in certain institutions requires an employer to obtain a police certificate before employing someone to work with minors. Whether it covers a self-employed private tutor, or an agency placing tutors: not verified.
Private tutoring is not a licensed occupation as far as the author knows; some course types (for example driving lessons) are regulated. Not verified.
Consumer protection: cancellation of distance transactions with capped fees, and specific rules for cancelling courses and ongoing services. Not verified in detail.
Displayed consumer prices must include VAT: believed true; not verified. Spam law (section 30A of the Communications Law): not verified in detail.

groups.heading: European Union and United Kingdom
items: GDPR and UK GDPR: children's data needs care; for online services offered directly to children, parental consent is needed below an age set by each country (13 to 16; 13 in the UK). Believed true; details not verified.

UK: criminal-record checks (DBS) are available for work with children; whether a self-employed private tutor is required to have one: believed not required by law, but expected. Not verified. One reference states its tutors are DBS-checked (observed 2026-11-22).

UK: English language schools may be accredited by the British Council; one reference states that a low-cost evening offer is not accredited and is taught by trainee teachers (observed 2026-11-22). The accreditation scheme's rules: not verified.

Cookies: consent for non-essential cookies (ePrivacy, PECR). One reference shows an "if you continue we will assume you are happy" notice (observed 2026-11-22); whether that wording is valid consent under UK rules is believed not, but not verified.

Distance contracts: 14-day cancellation right for many online purchases; exceptions for leisure services on a specific date and for digital content once access starts with consent. How they apply to a course run or a lesson pack: not verified.
Accessibility: the European Accessibility Act from June 2025, microenterprise exemption; scope not verified.

groups.heading: United States
items: COPPA (federal) regulates online collection of personal information from children under 13. Believed true; details not verified.
FERPA covers schools that receive federal funding, not private tutors. Not verified.
Background checks for tutors are generally a matter of state law and contract. Not verified per state.
Some states regulate private vocational schools and require approval before offering certain courses. Not verified per state.
The Americans with Disabilities Act is applied by courts to business websites in many cases; one reference links an accessibility page from its footer (observed 2026-11-22). Not verified.

platform_rules: The product may generate the structure of a privacy page (with a children's data heading), terms with cancellation and refunds, a safeguarding statement and an accessibility statement, each marked as a draft that needs review.
The product never states that the site "complies with" a named law, or that tutors are "checked" or "qualified", unless the customer confirms it (mandatory fact 13).
The product asks which country the provider is in before generating any legal page.

groups.heading: Applies almost everywhere
items: Guest data is personal data of private people. Names, households, dietary needs (possibly health data), attendance. Collect the least, protect the page, delete after the wedding.

A couple is a private person, not a business. Data-protection law often exempts purely personal activity, but publishing personal data on an open website may fall outside that exemption. Treat guests' data as if the law applies. Not verified per jurisdiction.
Children: names and photos of children deserve extra care; a parent's consent before publishing.
Cash gifts by payment link may involve payment-service rules and tax questions. Not verified.
For venues and planners: privacy notice, terms (deposits, cancellation, date changes, damage, noise and curfew), and consumer law on advertised prices.

groups.heading: Israel
items: A business website serving the public needs an accessibility statement under the Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law regulations, with size exemptions. Whether a couple's private site is in scope: believed not, not verified.
Event venues need a business licence and have capacity limits set by authorities. Not verified.
Prices advertised to consumers must include VAT. Per-guest pricing displays: not verified.
Privacy Protection Law, Amendment 13 (in force August 2025): what it requires of a venue's enquiry form: not verified.
Legal validity of a marriage ceremony is governed separately (religious authorities, recognition of marriages abroad). The site never states that a ceremony is legally binding. Not verified.

groups.heading: European Union and United Kingdom
items: GDPR and UK GDPR for venue enquiries and, likely, for a couple's public RSVP site (see "private person" above). Not verified.

UK: legal ceremonies may be held only at approved premises (England and Wales rules changed recently to allow outdoor ceremonies at approved venues). Whether a venue states it holds a licence is a fact to ask. Not verified.
Consumer rights on venue deposits and cancellation: national rules; withdrawal-right exceptions for dated leisure services are believed to apply. Not verified.
UK drip-pricing rules (DMCC Act 2024): how they apply to venue "from" prices: not verified.

groups.heading: United States
items: State law on deposits and cancellation; venue alcohol licensing; no single federal rule for a couple's site. Not verified.
ADA applies to venues as public accommodations. Not verified for websites.
